- [TEMPORAL] Session Date: 2023/06/02 (Fri) 09:08
- [USER] User asked for a simple classroom experiment to illustrate the anchoring effect.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant suggested a simple classroom experiment to illustrate the anchoring effect involving a dice, two pieces of paper, and a pen or pencil.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant provided the following materials for the experiment: a dice, two pieces of paper, and a pen or pencil.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant outlined the procedure for the experiment, which includes writing numbers 1 to 10 on one piece of paper and numbers 11 to 20 on another piece of paper.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant instructed to ask a volunteer to roll the dice and write down the number on a piece of paper in front of them.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant suggested asking the volunteer to guess the percentage of countries in the world that are members of the United Nations.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant directed the volunteer to add or subtract 10 from the number they rolled, depending on which piece of paper they chose.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant recommended asking the volunteer to guess the percentage of countries in the world that are members of the United Nations again after adjusting the number.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant advised recording the two guesses and calculating the average of the two.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant suggested asking the rest of the class to guess the percentage of countries in the world that are members of the United Nations without rolling the dice or looking at the pieces of paper.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant recommended comparing the class's guesses with the average of the volunteer's two guesses.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant explained that the anchoring effect occurs when people rely too heavily on the first piece of information they receive when making a decision.
- [USER] User asked for examples of Behavioral Law and Economics (BLE) studies using experiments run on Amazon Mechanical Turk platform.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant confirmed that there are many examples of BLE studies that have used experiments on Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk).
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant provided an example study titled "When Does Regulation Distort Values? Lessons from the Regulation of Kidney Exchange" by Alvin E. Roth and H. Umit Gurbuz, which investigated how regulations can affect values placed on goods and services.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant described that the kidney exchange study involved asking participants to indicate their willingness to pay for the chance to receive a kidney transplant under different regulatory regimes.
